Question six. What is maximum likelihood estimation, or M L E? Choose the parameter that makes the data you saw most probable. Twelve clicks in forty views: across every possible click rate, the likelihood peaks at point three, the share you saw. Ten times the data keeps the peak and narrows the curve. Its width is the precision. For a normal mean, the M L E is just the sample mean, and logistic regression is fit the same way, by maximizing the likelihood of the labels. Question seven. What makes an estimator unbiased? Its average over many samples equals the true value. The sample mean is unbiased. Variance divided by n is not: each sample's spread is measured from its own mean, which sits closer to its data than the true mean does, so the squares come out small. With five values, it runs about twenty percent low. Dividing by n minus one fixes it.

Question eight. What does a ninety-five percent confidence interval, or C I, actually mean? It describes the procedure, not one interval. Take a hundred samples, build an interval from each, and about ninety-five of them catch the true mean. Here, ninety-four do, and six miss. So it isn't a ninety-five percent chance that the mean is in this interval. The mean is fixed. The interval is what's random, and any one of them either contains the mean or it doesn't. The biggest block is next: eight questions on testing.
